description: Before Zeus, his father Cronus devoured his own children. Here is how the void gave birth to the gods of Olympus.

hero.hook: Before Olympus, the world was born out of emptiness, violence, and family coups.

blocks.text: Before the gods of **Olympus** ruled, Greek myth imagined an original emptiness: **Chaos**. It was not noisy disorder. It was a gap, an abyss, and life came surging out of it.

The birth of the gods was not gentle. It was a chain of crises and power grabs. The poet **Hesiod** told the story in the 8th century BC, in [[Hesiod's Theogony]]. Here is how the world went from emptiness to the court of **Zeus**.
**Chaos** first produced forces with no human face. **Gaia**, the Earth, offered solid ground. **Tartarus** was a deep prison below the world. **Eros**, desire, let beings join together.

blocks.caption: Gaia, the Earth, the first power of the Greek world

blocks.text: Gaia gave birth to **Uranus**, the starry Sky, on her own. Together they produced the **Titans**, gods of raw strength, and monsters: the **Cyclopes** and the **Hecatoncheires**, giants with a hundred arms.
For the Greeks, the world did not come out of nothing. It came out of a separation: the space between Sky and Earth finally left room for life.
Uranus hated his children. He shut them inside Gaia's body. The Earth was suffocating. The first revolution of the cosmos was coming.

sections.title: From Chaos came Earth and Sky

blocks.text: Gaia forged a sickle out of [[adamant]], a legendary metal of absolute hardness. Only the youngest Titan, the cunning **Cronus**, agreed to act. Hidden in his mother's side, he castrated Uranus and split Sky from Earth forever.
Cronus became king. But the blood of Uranus went on fertilizing the world: it produced the **Erinyes**, goddesses of family vengeance, and **Aphrodite**, goddess of love, who rose from the sea foam.
The name **Aphrodite** comes from the Greek “aphros”, which means “foam”. Her birth recalls the crime that opened the reign of Cronus.

A prophecy threatened Cronus: one of his sons would dethrone him. To prevent it, he swallowed each child at birth, **Hestia**, **Demeter**, **Hera**, **Hades**, **Poseidon**. The Greek gods had very human fears, and that is [[Greek divine anthropomorphism]].

**Rhea**, wife of Cronus, refused to lose her last child. She handed him a stone wrapped in swaddling clothes. The real baby, **Zeus**, grew up in secret in the cave of [[Dicté]], in Crete. The [[Curetes]], sacred warriors, drowned out his crying with their shouts. The goat **Amalthea** fed him.

As an adult, Zeus forced Cronus to disgorge his brothers and sisters. They came back out ready to fight. So began the **Titanomachy**, a ten-year war between the Titans and the future Olympians. The Cyclopes gave Zeus the decisive weapon: the **thunderbolt**.

blocks.text: The Titans were thrown into Tartarus. **Zeus** took the Sky, **Poseidon** the seas, **Hades** the world of the dead. **Olympus** became a divine court, better ordered than the raw force of the Titans.

sections.title: Zeus frees his brothers and sisters

blocks.text: Even as the winner, Zeus stayed anxious. He married **Metis**, Wisdom, then swallowed her for fear of a stronger son. Out of that act came **Athena**, who sprang fully armed from her father's skull: strategy became the pillar of power.
The word **panic** comes from the god **Pan**. During a war against the Giants, his shout is said to have spread a sudden, unreasoning terror.

These myths do not turn the gods into models of virtue. They turn them into mirrors: jealousy, fear of being replaced, hunger to rule. From Chaos to Olympus, the Greeks told how civilization tries to master raw violence.
Greek myth moves from **Chaos** to the order of **Olympus** through one violent takeover after another. The gods share our passions, but not our mortality.
